topic: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Waves for detection and exploration (physics only) (HT only)
subject: physics

items.q: Waves are sent down into the ground to search for a hidden layer of rock, in which the waves would travel at a different speed. What happens where the waves reach the top of the hidden layer?
items.correct: Part of the wave is reflected and part carries on downwards
items.misconception: The wave carries on at exactly the same speed as before
items.why: Students learn a single quoted value for the speed of sound (about 330 m/s) or the speed of light early on and treat it as a property of the wave rather than of the wave in a particular medium. Speeds in solids and liquids are rarely quoted alongside it. Velocity is one of the three differences the specification names. It is precisely because a wave travels at a different speed in the hidden material that a boundary reflects part of the wave and can be detected. It also means the correct speed for that medium must be used when a time is turned into a distance.
items.random_wrong: The whole wave is reflected and none carries on downwards

items.q: In a survey, the waves pass easily through layer X but are strongly absorbed by layer Y, which lies beneath it. What effect does this have on the survey?
items.correct: Reflections from below layer Y are weak or missing at the detector
items.misconception: A strong reflection returns from layer Y because it absorbs waves
items.why: The everyday word 'absorb' suggests soaking something up and holding it, and students meet 'absorbed' and 'reflected' in the same list of things that happen at a surface, so the two get blurred. Absorption and reflection are different and are named separately by the specification. A strongly absorbing layer weakens or removes reflections from everything beneath it, which is why the wave chosen for a survey must be one that the material in between absorbs only weakly.
items.random_wrong: No reflections at all are received, even from the top of layer Y

items.q: Differences in which three properties, between different types of wave in solids and liquids, are used to detect and explore hidden structures?
items.correct: Velocity, absorption and reflection
items.misconception: Frequency, absorption and reflection
items.why: Students know something must change at a boundary, and frequency is the wave property they can name most readily. Everyday talk about signals 'changing frequency' reinforces it. The three differences the specification names are velocity, absorption and reflection. Detection depends on the change of velocity at the boundary, the partial reflection this produces, and the time that reflection takes to return — not on any change of frequency.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes ultrasound waves?
items.correct: Sound waves with a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing
items.misconception: Sound waves that are much louder than a human ear can safely hear
items.why: Everyday use of 'ultra' means extreme, and students routinely confuse frequency (pitch) with amplitude (loudness), which are separate wave properties. The definition is about frequency alone. A quiet ultrasound wave is still ultrasound; a very loud 500 Hz note is not, because 500 Hz is within the range of human hearing.
items.random_wrong: Electromagnetic waves used to make images of the inside of the body

items.q: An ultrasound pulse sent into the body meets three tissue boundaries one after another. Why can a reflection be received from all three?
items.correct: Only part of the pulse reflects at each boundary; the rest goes on
items.misconception: The pulse is reflected in full at each boundary that it reaches
items.why: Reflection is first met with light and plane mirrors, where almost all of the light comes back, and transmission is first met with clear glass, where almost all of it goes through. Students carry over an all-or-nothing picture. The specification states that ultrasound waves are partially reflected at a boundary between two different media. This is essential: if the first boundary reflected everything, nothing could be learned about anything deeper, and imaging would be impossible.
items.random_wrong: The pulse speeds up at each boundary, so it reaches them all

items.q: An ultrasound pulse is sent into a steel block to look for a crack. Ultrasound travels at 6000 m/s in the steel. A reflection from the crack is received 0.000 040 s after the pulse is sent. How far below the surface is the crack?
items.why: Students apply distance = speed × time correctly but do not picture the path. The time is the one quantity given in the question, so it is used without asking what journey it belongs to. What is timed is a reflection, so the time covers the journey to the boundary and the journey back. Work out speed × time first, then halve it to get the distance to the boundary. Halving is the step examiners look for.

items.q: A pulse of ultrasound is sent into a steel casting. From one region a reflection returns much sooner than the reflection from the far side of the casting. What is the best conclusion?
items.correct: A boundary such as a crack lies inside that region
items.misconception: The ultrasound was completely absorbed in that region
items.why: The everyday word 'absorb' suggests soaking something up and holding it, and students meet 'absorbed' and 'reflected' in the same list of things that happen at a surface, so the two get blurred. Absorption and reflection are different and are named separately by the specification. A strongly absorbing layer weakens or removes reflections from everything beneath it, which is why the wave chosen for a survey must be one that the material in between absorbs only weakly.
items.random_wrong: The casting must be thicker in that region than elsewhere

items.q: Which statement explains how an ultrasound scan builds up an image of a structure inside the body?
items.correct: Reflections from boundaries between tissues arrive at different times
items.misconception: Ultrasound is absorbed by bone, casting a shadow onto a film
items.why: Both are met as 'scans' in a medical context, and both are described as passing into the body. The prefix 'ultra' also echoes 'ultraviolet', which is electromagnetic. Ultrasound waves are sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. An ultrasound image is built from reflections timed at a detector, not from radiation passing through the body onto a film.
items.random_wrong: Ultrasound is completely reflected by the first tissue it meets

items.q: Which statement correctly describes P-waves and S-waves?
items.correct: P-waves are longitudinal and S-waves are transverse
items.misconception: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal
items.why: The two labels are arbitrary letters with nothing in them to cue the answer, so a student with no memory hook has an even chance of swapping them. The swap then corrupts every conclusion drawn afterwards. Fix the pairing first: P for longitudinal (a push wave, like sound), S for transverse (a shake wave, side to side). The rest of the topic depends on it, because it is the transverse S-wave that cannot travel through a liquid.
items.random_wrong: Both are longitudinal, like all waves in solid rock

items.q: Which statement about seismic waves travelling through the Earth is correct?
items.correct: S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, but P-waves can
items.misconception: Neither S-waves nor P-waves can travel through any liquid
items.why: Students remember 'liquid blocks seismic waves' as a single simplified rule instead of the distinction the specification draws between the two wave types. The contrast between the two is the whole point. If liquid stopped both, no wave would arrive from the far side of the Earth and there would be nothing to compare. It is because P-waves arrive and S-waves do not that a liquid region can be identified.
items.random_wrong: S-waves can travel through any liquid, but P-waves cannot

items.q: After an earthquake, detectors on the far side of the Earth receive P-waves but no S-waves. What does this provide evidence for?
items.correct: Part of the core is liquid, so S-waves cannot pass through it
items.misconception: The core is a hollow space with no material inside it at all
items.why: Students know a wave that fails to arrive has been blocked, and the most vivid picture of 'nothing there' is a hole. The role of P-waves, which do arrive, is overlooked. P-waves cross the core and are detected, so the core is certainly not empty. The specific fact that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid is what makes their absence evidence for a liquid region.
items.random_wrong: S-waves are transverse, so they cannot travel through a solid

items.q: How do P-waves provide evidence about the size of the Earth's core?
items.correct: Their speed changes at the core boundary, bending their paths
items.misconception: They cannot enter the core, so a total shadow is produced
items.why: Students remember 'liquid blocks seismic waves' as a single simplified rule instead of the distinction the specification draws between the two wave types. The contrast between the two is the whole point. If liquid stopped both, no wave would arrive from the far side of the Earth and there would be nothing to compare. It is because P-waves arrive and S-waves do not that a liquid region can be identified.
items.random_wrong: They travel at one steady speed everywhere inside the Earth

items.q: A P-wave travels through solid rock. How does the rock move as the wave passes?
items.correct: Parallel to the direction in which the wave travels
items.misconception: At right angles to the direction the wave travels
items.why: The two labels are arbitrary letters with nothing in them to cue the answer, so a student with no memory hook has an even chance of swapping them. The swap then corrupts every conclusion drawn afterwards. Fix the pairing first: P for longitudinal (a push wave, like sound), S for transverse (a shake wave, side to side). The rest of the topic depends on it, because it is the transverse S-wave that cannot travel through a liquid.
items.random_wrong: The rock itself is carried along with the wave

items.q: Which statement about echo sounding is correct?
items.correct: High frequency sound is used to find depth and locate objects
items.misconception: Radio pulses are used because they travel well through water
items.why: Radar and light-based rangefinders are familiar from the air, and students do not meet the fact that water is a strong absorber of both. This is exactly the use of the differences in absorption that the specification refers to. High frequency sound travels well through water and reflects from the sea bed and from objects in it, so echo sounding uses sound.
items.random_wrong: Light pulses are used because light travels fastest in water

items.q: A ship uses echo sounding to measure the depth of the sea. The speed of the sound waves in the sea water is 1500 m/s and the echo from the sea bed returns 0.80 s after the pulse is sent out. How deep is the water?
items.why: Students apply distance = speed × time correctly but do not picture the path. The time is the one quantity given in the question, so it is used without asking what journey it belongs to. What is timed is a reflection, so the time covers the journey to the boundary and the journey back. Work out speed × time first, then halve it to get the distance to the boundary. Halving is the step examiners look for.

items.q: Echo sounding uses high frequency sound waves rather than light or radio waves. Why?
items.correct: Water absorbs light and radio waves much more strongly than sound
items.misconception: Light and radio pulses would work just as well at any depth
items.why: Radar and light-based rangefinders are familiar from the air, and students do not meet the fact that water is a strong absorber of both. This is exactly the use of the differences in absorption that the specification refers to. High frequency sound travels well through water and reflects from the sea bed and from objects in it, so echo sounding uses sound.
items.random_wrong: Sound travels faster through sea water than light does

items.q: Why was the study of seismic waves so important for our knowledge of the Earth?
items.correct: It gave new evidence about regions nobody can observe directly
items.misconception: It confirmed what had already been seen by drilling to the core
items.why: Samples of rock and drilling are familiar from geology lessons, and diagrams of the Earth's layers are drawn with such confidence that they look like something someone has seen. The core has never been reached or sampled. The specification's point is precisely that the study of seismic waves provided new evidence which led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.
items.random_wrong: It proved that the inside of the Earth cannot be studied at all

items.q: Measurements of seismic waves led scientists to conclude that part of the Earth's core is liquid. This conclusion is an example of scientists:
items.correct: using indirect evidence to reach a conclusion about a hidden region
items.misconception: taking samples of the core from very deep mines and boreholes
items.why: Samples of rock and drilling are familiar from geology lessons, and diagrams of the Earth's layers are drawn with such confidence that they look like something someone has seen. The core has never been reached or sampled. The specification's point is precisely that the study of seismic waves provided new evidence which led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.
items.random_wrong: guessing, because a hidden region cannot be studied by evidence

items.q: Ultrasound is outside the range of human hearing — is it above or below it?
items.correct: Above. Ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans.
items.misconception: Ultrasound is sound that is too low for people to hear, below the bottom of the hearing range.
items.why: Students remember only that ultrasound is 'outside what we can hear' and then guess the wrong end of the range, or confuse it with infrasound, which is genuinely below the lower limit. The specification is explicit: higher than the upper limit of hearing. With the range of human hearing given as 20 Hz to 20 kHz, ultrasound is above 20 kHz.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do P-waves travel at one steady speed all the way through the Earth?
items.correct: No. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so their speed changes as they pass through different regions.
items.misconception: P-waves have a fixed speed, so their arrival times tell you only how far away the earthquake was.
items.why: Speed is usually treated as a single given number in calculations, and a picture of the Earth's interior as uniform makes a changing speed seem unnecessary. The specification states directly that P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. These speed changes at boundaries alter the paths the waves follow, and that is a large part of the evidence for the size and structure of the core.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: As a seismic wave passes through rock, does the rock travel with it?
items.correct: No. The rock oscillates about its position; the wave transfers energy through the rock without transferring the rock itself.
items.misconception: The wave carries the rock along with it, which is why the ground moves in an earthquake.
items.why: Earthquake footage shows the ground visibly moving and objects being carried, and students transfer the idea of a moving substance to the wave itself. In a P-wave the rock oscillates back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels; in an S-wave it oscillates at right angles to that direction. In both, the material returns to where it started and only energy is transferred onwards.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does sound travel faster than light through water?
items.correct: No. Light travels far faster than sound in water; sound is used because it is absorbed much less, not because it is faster.
items.misconception: Sound is used underwater because sound goes faster in water than light does.
items.why: Students learn that sound travels faster in water than in air and turn this into a general claim that sound is fast in water. Speed is also the reason they are readiest to reach for. Speed is not the reason. The reason echo sounding uses high frequency sound is that water absorbs sound weakly and absorbs light and radio waves strongly, so only the sound pulse returns from the sea bed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If nobody can observe the core, is what we say about it just a guess?
items.correct: No. It is a conclusion drawn from measurements of real waves that have passed through the Earth — indirect evidence, not guesswork.
items.misconception: Anything you cannot see for yourself cannot really be known, so the liquid core is just a theory somebody made up.
items.why: Students equate evidence with seeing, and the everyday use of 'theory' to mean 'hunch' encourages them to treat an indirectly supported conclusion as unsupported. Indirect evidence is still evidence. Detectors record which waves arrive, when, and from which directions; those measurements can only be explained by particular structures inside the Earth. This is how discoveries were made about parts of the Earth that are not directly observable.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
